passages.title: Renovating a Flat
passages.text:
When Linh bought her first flat in Hanoi, it looked tired and old. The previous owner had left a dirty brown **carpet** in the living room, and the windows had no **blinds**, so strangers could see inside. The first job was the bathroom, where cracked wall **tile** hid a leak. She replaced it with fresh white pieces and then moved on to the kitchen. A rusty **kitchen sink** stood under the window, and it leaked every time she turned on the tap, so a plumber fitted a new one in a day.

The next weekend she chose new **floor tiles** for the hall; they were cool and easy to clean, which suited the hot climate. In the corner of the kitchen she placed **a fridge-freezer**, tall enough to store a week of food for her family. Finally, she turned to the living room. After a long search she found **a big soft sofa** in a sale and put it by the window. When her friends came to visit, they all agreed that the flat now felt like a real home.

passages.title: Living with Flatmates
passages.text:
Living with other students is cheaper, but it is not always easy. In my first year at university I had to **share a bedroom** with a boy named Tom. At first it felt strange, and the early weeks were **unpleasant** because we argued about noise and tidiness. Tom was also a little **mean** with money; he never bought milk or soap for the flat, although he used everything.

One evening, however, we cooked together and talked for hours. That night we decided to **have dinner in the dining room** every Sunday with our other flatmates, and the habit slowly changed the atmosphere. We also made a rota so that everyone could **use the washing machine** fairly, one person at a time. Our **current** flat is much calmer than the old one, and Tom is now one of my closest friends. Looking back, the awkward start did not matter, because **we’ve been mates ever since**.

passages.title: Money Matters
passages.text:
Minh was twenty-five and had just started his first job. He had one small problem: he still **owed** his cousin two million dong for a laptop. A friend advised him to visit the bank and **deposit** part of his salary each month. The bank offered a special savings account with a high interest rate, and an adviser explained the rules to him.

Customers must **agree not to withdraw** the money for twelve months, and the offer would **run out** at the end of the month. "**That sounds reasonable to me**," Minh said, after thinking carefully. **In the short term**, he would have less spending money and could not **engage in** expensive hobbies such as weekend trips. But **in the long term**, the savings would grow and give him the freedom to buy a flat of his own. Minh signed the form, paid back his cousin first, and left the bank feeling proud of his plan.

passages.title: A Saturday at the Mall
passages.text:
Last Saturday I went to the new **shopping centre** near my house because my brother needed a bag for school. I wanted something strong, so I chose a blue **rucksack** with lots of pockets. At the same time, I noticed a shop offering socks at **three for the price of two**, so I took six pairs. My old ones are full of holes, and I **hardly ever wear** them now.

There was a long **queue** at the till, and I waited for almost ten minutes. When I reached the front, the assistant said, "Can I check your card **real quick**?" I handed it over and said, "**Here you go**." She scanned everything and put it all in a paper bag. "And **there you go**," she said with a smile, giving me back my card. I walked home feeling pleased: I had saved money, and I had a useful present for my brother.

passages.title: A Seaside Weekend
passages.text:
My uncle lives in a small fishing village in Cornwall, and I spent a weekend there last summer. There is no cinema or nightclub, so **there isn't much to do** in the evenings. **Apart from** walking along the beach, most visitors just sit in cafés and watch the boats. However, the food is wonderful.

On Saturday morning we bought a fresh **mackerel** straight from a fisherman, and my uncle showed me how to cook it. He asked me to wash a **courgette** from his garden and to **cut** it **into pieces** while he lit the grill. I usually **have problems with** cooking, so I was nervous, but the recipe was **reasonably** simple. We seasoned the fish with salt and a little lemon, and ten minutes later we were eating on the harbour wall. The fish and vegetables tasted delicious, and I decided that a quiet village is not boring if the food is this good.

passages.title: Lost on the Way to Da Lat
passages.text:
Last month I drove to Da Lat for a job interview, and I was very nervous. I was **on my way to** the city centre when I decided to **go via** a small town to avoid the traffic. It was a bad idea. The road had several branches, and at the first **turning** I was not sure which side to choose. I **took the wrong turning** and soon realised that I was climbing into the mountains.

I did not want to **get lost** in the dark, so I stopped at a petrol station and **asked** the owner **the way** to the centre. Instead of explaining, the kind man walked outside and **directed** me **to** the main street with his hand. "Just **follow signs to** the lake," he said. Twenty minutes later I arrived, tired but on time. Now I always check the map before I leave home.

passages.title: A Narrow Escape
passages.text:
If you ever **see an accident**, you will understand how quickly things can go wrong. Last Tuesday I was standing at a bus stop beside **the main road** when I noticed a delivery van speeding towards a crossing. A boy on a bicycle was **approaching** the same junction from the left. The van driver saw him too late. He **braked hard**, but the wet surface made the van slide.

To avoid the boy, the driver **swerved** sharply to the right and **crashed into** a lamp post. There was a loud bang, and for a moment everyone on the street stood still. Fortunately, both the boy and the driver were fine. The driver admitted that it was the second time he had **had an accident** this year, and he promised to drive more slowly in future. I walked home thinking that safety on the road depends on patience.

passages.title: Safer Streets Near Schools
passages.text:
Parents near Greenfield **primary school** have asked the council to make their street safer. Last month a driver lost control and drove up onto the **pavement**, where children from the nearby **nursery school** usually walk each morning. Luckily, nobody was there at the time, but the car hit **a parked car** and caused serious **damage to** two garden fences.

Residents say the next accident could **injure** a child. The street is narrow, and the school gate is **on the opposite side of the road** from the main car park, so families have to cross twice a day. The council has promised to build a crossing and lower the speed limit. "We cannot wait for a tragedy," said one mother, who walks her four-year-old to nursery every day. A decision will be announced at a public meeting next week, and everyone in the area is welcome.

passages.title: Going to School in Britain
passages.text:
In Britain most children attend a **state school**, which is free and paid for by the government. A smaller number go to a **private school**, where parents pay fees. Some private schools **are operated by** charities or religious groups, while others belong to companies. At sixteen, students **take exams** called GCSEs, usually **in up to ten subjects**.

After that, they can **stay at school** for two more years to prepare for university, or they can leave to start a job or training. Teachers say that the most successful pupils are not always the cleverest; they are the ones who **learn from their mistakes** and listen to advice. Regular practice helps students **make progress** even in difficult subjects. At the end of each term, parents often ask how their children **get on**, and a short school report gives them the answer. This system is not perfect, but it gives young people several routes into adult life.
